techniques.name: Monte Carlo Dropout
techniques.description: Monte Carlo dropout estimates how uncertain a neural network is about each prediction. Dropout randomly switches off some of the network's units and is normally used only in training, but here it stays on at prediction time. Each forward pass (one run of an input through the network) therefore uses a different random pattern of units, and the input is run through typically tens to a hundred times. The average gives the prediction, and the spread across runs is read as epistemic uncertainty, meaning uncertainty from the model's limited knowledge rather than noise in the data. The method approximates Bayesian inference, but the spread is an estimate whose reliability should be checked against held-out errors.

example_use_cases.description: Quantifying diagnostic uncertainty in medical imaging models by running 50+ Monte Carlo forward passes to detect when a chest X-ray classification is highly uncertain, prompting radiologist review for borderline cases.

An autonomous-driving team replays recorded camera footage through its object detector with dropout left on, and finds the scenes (night rain, unusual vehicles) where detections vary most between passes. It uses them to decide what data to collect and which scenarios to add to simulation testing.

A grid operator's demand-forecasting network, trained with dropout, is run 100 times each morning. Days on which the forecasts spread beyond the planners' tolerance are sent for human review before reserve capacity is booked.

limitations.description: The spread across passes reflects uncertainty about the model's parameters, not noise in the data that varies from input to input. An input in a very noisy region can still show a narrow spread, so a narrow spread does not mean the outcome is predictable.

Each prediction needs many forward passes, typically 50 to 100, so inference costs that many times more compute, and too few passes make the spread itself unstable. The passes can run in parallel, which limits added delay but not total compute, so real-time or edge deployments with tight budgets may not afford it.

The network must have been trained with dropout, and the derivation assumes it sits before every weight layer. A model trained without dropout has to be retrained, so the technique is often unavailable for models already built or bought in.

The size of the spread depends on the dropout probability and weight decay, which the developer sets or tunes on validation data rather than learns from the data. The uncertainty scale is partly a design choice and needs checking against held-out errors.

The spread is an approximation, and its behaviour depends on the architecture. In the original paper's regression experiments, uncertainty kept growing away from the training data with ReLU activations but stayed bounded with TanH, so a narrow spread on unfamiliar inputs is not proof of familiarity.

resources.title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
resources.abstract: Deep learning tools have gained tremendous attention in applied machine learning. However such tools for regression and classification do not capture model uncertainty. In comparison, Bayesian models offer a mathematically grounded framework to reason about model uncertainty, but usually come with a prohibitive computational cost. In this paper we develop a new theoretical framework casting dropout training in deep neural networks (NNs) as approximate Bayesian inference in deep Gaussian processes. A direct result of this theory gives us tools to model uncertainty with dropout NNs -- extracting information from existing models that has been thrown away so far. This mitigates the problem of representing uncertainty in deep learning without sacrificing either computational complexity or test accuracy. We perform an extensive study of the properties of dropout's uncertainty. Various network architectures and non-linearities are assessed on tasks of regression and classification, using MNIST as an example. We show a considerable improvement in predictive log-likelihood and RMSE compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and finish by using dropout's uncertainty in deep reinforcement learning.

Leveraging uncertainty information from deep neural networks for disease detection
resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) has revolutionized the field of computer vision and image processing. In medical imaging, algorithmic solutions based on DL have been shown to achieve high performance on tasks that previously required medical experts. However, DL-based solutions for disease detection have been proposed without methods to quantify and control their uncertainty in a decision. In contrast, a physician knows whether she is uncertain about a case and will consult more experienced colleagues if needed. Here we evaluate drop-out based Bayesian uncertainty measures for DL in diagnosing diabetic retinopathy (DR) from fundus images and show that it captures uncertainty better than straightforward alternatives. Furthermore, we show that uncertainty informed decision referral can improve diagnostic performance. Experiments across different networks, tasks and datasets show robust generalization. Depending on network capacity and task/dataset difficulty, we surpass 85% sensitivity and 80% specificity as recommended by the NHS when referring 0−20% of the most uncertain decisions for further inspection. We analyse causes of uncertainty by relating intuitions from 2D visualizations to the high-dimensional image space. While uncertainty is sensitive to clinically relevant cases, sensitivity to unfamiliar data samples is task dependent, but can be rendered more robust.

techniques.name: Out-of-Distribution Detector for Neural Networks
techniques.description: ODIN (Out-of-Distribution Detector for Neural Networks) flags inputs that look unlike the data a neural network classifier was trained on, and it works on an already trained network without retraining it. A classifier reports a confidence score, the highest probability it gives to any class, but that score is often high even for unfamiliar inputs. ODIN adjusts the score in two ways so that familiar and unfamiliar inputs separate better. It divides the classifier's raw output scores by a large constant, called the temperature, before turning them into probabilities, and it nudges the input slightly in the direction that raises the score, which lifts familiar inputs more than unfamiliar ones. An input whose adjusted score falls below a chosen threshold is flagged as out-of-distribution, so its prediction can be withheld or referred for review.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital screens each chest X-ray with ODIN before the diagnostic classifier's result is shown. Scans that are not chest X-rays, or that carry heavy artefacts, are flagged for human review instead of receiving a confident diagnosis, and the false positive rate is measured on a sample of such scans first.

An automated driving team scores each camera frame with ODIN and passes frames below the threshold to a fallback routine, such as slowing the vehicle and requesting remote assistance. The team measures how many unfamiliar frames, such as sensor faults or unusual scenes, are wrongly accepted before relying on the detector.

limitations.description: Temperature and perturbation size are tuned on a validation set that includes out-of-distribution examples, so some representative unfamiliar data is needed before deployment. The paper found settings transferred reasonably between validation sets, but only on image benchmarks.

Detection gets harder as unfamiliar inputs resemble the training data. In the original paper, at 95% acceptance of familiar images, the share of unfamiliar natural images wrongly accepted rose from at most about 11% with a 10-class training set to between 19% and 58% with a 100-class one, so performance must be measured on the deployment's own data.
Not designed to resist inputs deliberately crafted to look in-distribution, and the original paper does not evaluate adversarial evasion, so it gives no protection against a deliberate attacker.
Needs access to the network's gradients to compute the input perturbation, so it cannot be applied to a model that is reachable only through an API.
Each input needs at least one extra forward pass and one backward pass before the final scoring pass, which can matter for real-time or high-volume use.

resources.title: Enhancing The Reliability of Out-of-distribution Image Detection in Neural Networks
resources.abstract: We consider the problem of detecting out-of-distribution images in neural networks. We propose ODIN, a simple and effective method that does not require any change to a pre-trained neural network. Our method is based on the observation that using temperature scaling and adding small perturbations to the input can separate the softmax score distributions between in- and out-of-distribution images, allowing for more effective detection. We show in a series of experiments that ODIN is compatible with diverse network architectures and datasets. It consistently outperforms the baseline approach by a large margin, establishing a new state-of-the-art performance on this task. For example, ODIN reduces the false positive rate from the baseline 34.7% to 4.3% on the DenseNet (applied to CIFAR-10) when the true positive rate is 95%.

resources.title: Confidence-Based Out-of-Distribution Detection: A Comparative Study and Analysis
resources.abstract: Image classification models deployed in the real world may receive inputs outside the intended data distribution. For critical applications such as clinical decision making, it is important that a model can detect such out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs and express its uncertainty. In this work, we assess the capability of various state-of-the-art approaches for confidence-based OOD detection through a comparative study and in-depth analysis. First, we leverage a computer vision benchmark to reproduce and compare multiple OOD detection methods. We then evaluate their capabilities on the challenging task of disease classification using chest X-rays. Our study shows that high performance in a computer vision task does not directly translate to accuracy in a medical imaging task. We analyse factors that affect performance of the methods between the two tasks. Our results provide useful insights for developing the next generation of OOD detection methods.

sample_claims.text: Camera frames that fall outside the perception network's training distribution, such as those from a sensor fault, are flagged before the planner uses the network's output.
Scans that are not of the type the diagnostic classifier was trained on are rejected by the out-of-distribution detector instead of receiving a confident diagnosis.
The detector's threshold is set so that 95% of in-distribution validation inputs are accepted, and the share of out-of-distribution test inputs wrongly accepted at that threshold is reported.
Images of unfamiliar part types or from unfamiliar cameras are held for human inspection instead of passing through the automated quality-control classifier.

techniques.name: Temperature Scaling
techniques.description: Temperature scaling is a correction applied after training to a classifier that is more confident than it is accurate, a common problem in modern neural networks. It divides the model's raw scores (logits) by a single number, the temperature, before they are turned into probabilities, so a temperature above one lowers confidence and one below one raises it. The temperature is fitted on a labelled validation set kept apart from training by minimising negative log-likelihood, a measure that penalises confident wrong answers, and the model's own weights are not changed. Because dividing by one positive number never changes which class scores highest, predictions and accuracy stay the same. Stated confidence usually moves much closer to observed accuracy on data like the validation set, which a reliability diagram (a chart of stated confidence against how often the model was right) can show, but some miscalibration remains.

example_use_cases.description: A trust-and-safety team auto-removes posts only when its neural text classifier reports at least 95% confidence. The team fits a temperature on one labelled validation set, then checks on a second, unseen labelled set that posts scored near 95% really are abusive about 95% of the time, and adjusts the removal threshold if they are not.

An environmental agency's land-cover classifier was trained on summer satellite images and is now used on winter scenes, where it is overconfident. The team fits a fresh temperature on a small labelled winter sample and compares calibration error before and after on separate winter test scenes, rather than reusing the summer temperature.

A hospital radiology department displays the model's confidence beside each chest X-ray finding. Before display, the team fits a temperature on held-out scans from its own hospital and reports expected calibration error on a test set, so that clinicians can read a displayed 70% as roughly 70 correct findings in 100 similar cases.

limitations.description: A single temperature is fitted for the whole dataset, so it corrects average overconfidence but not differences between groups or regions of the input space. A minority group can stay overconfident while overall calibration looks good, and only a per-group calibration check shows it.

It leaves predicted classes unchanged, so accuracy and the model's mistakes stay as they were. A weak model remains weak and only becomes more honest about it, so calibration cannot substitute for improving the model.

The temperature is fitted on data resembling the training distribution, and calibration can degrade when deployment data shifts. In one large benchmark, error in stated confidence rose significantly as shift increased, even though it was low on unshifted data.

It needs labelled held-out data that resembles deployment, separate from the training data, and a further separate set to measure the result, because scoring calibration on the data used to fit the temperature flatters it. Small datasets may not leave enough for both.

Calibration is judged on the confidence of the predicted class only. The probabilities given to the other classes are not checked by that measure, so uses that read the whole probability list, such as ranking several likely diagnoses, need separate testing.

resources.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Confidence calibration -- the problem of predicting probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood -- is important for classification models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. Through extensive experiments, we observe that depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normalization are important factors influencing calibration. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art architectures with image and document classification datasets. Our analysis and experiments not only offer insights into neural network learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling -- a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling -- is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions.

Calibrating the credit risk model with a single temperature left its predicted classes, and therefore its accuracy, unchanged, while its default probabilities now track the observed default rates on held-out data.
A displayed confidence of 80% corresponds to about 80 correct predictions in 100, as shown by a reliability diagram on data not used to fit the temperature.
After refitting the temperature on a labelled sample from the new region, the land-cover classifier's calibration error on that region's test data is no worse than on the original region.

techniques.name: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve
techniques.description: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) summarises how well a classifier finds the cases that matter when those cases are rare. Precision is the share of positive predictions that are correct, and recall is the share of actual positives that are found. Plotting one against the other at every classification threshold gives a curve, and AUPRC is the area under it, from 0 to 1. Neither precision nor recall uses true negatives, so a large majority class does not flatter the score as it can flatter accuracy and AUC-ROC. A model with no skill scores about the proportion of positives in the data, so the score is only meaningful next to that baseline.

example_use_cases.description: A payments team compares candidate fraud models on a held-out month of transactions in which about 1 in 500 is fraudulent. It ranks them by AUPRC against the 0.2% no-skill baseline, then reads the best model's curve to choose a threshold that keeps false alarms within what the investigation team can review.

A hospital evaluates a model that screens for a rare condition affecting about 1 in 200 patients. ROC AUC can look high even when most flagged patients are healthy, so the team reports AUPRC against the 0.5% baseline and reads the precision at the recall clinicians require, to decide whether the follow-up workload is manageable.

A manufacturer compares two defect-detection models for a production line where about 1 in 1,000 parts is faulty. It uses AUPRC on a labelled validation batch to choose between them, so that a model is not preferred simply for labelling nearly every good part correctly.

limitations.description: AUPRC depends on the share of positives in the data, so scores from datasets or groups with different proportions cannot be compared directly, and no universal pass mark can be set. Each score has to be read against its own no-skill baseline, which is about the positive proportion.

It treats one class as the positive class and ignores true negatives, so it says nothing about how reliably the model clears the majority class. That matters where certifying a case as negative or safe is as important as catching positives.

A single area averages over every threshold, including ones no deployment would use, and can hide poor precision at the recall the application needs. Choosing the operating point needs a look at that part of the curve and the cost of each kind of error.

The area can be computed in different ways. Trapezoidal linear interpolation between points gives an overly optimistic value, whereas step-wise average precision does not, so scores from different libraries or settings may not match.
Few positive test cases make precision-recall estimates unstable, so a high score from a small sample may not hold on a larger, representative evaluation set.

resources.title: The relationship between Precision-Recall and ROC curves
resources.abstract: Receiver Operator Characteristic (ROC) curves are commonly used to present results for binary decision problems in machine learning. However, when dealing with highly skewed datasets, Precision-Recall (PR) curves give a more informative picture of an algorithm's performance. We show that a deep connection exists between ROC space and PR space, such that a curve dominates in ROC space if and only if it dominates in PR space. A corollary is the notion of an achievable PR curve, which has properties much like the convex hull in ROC space; we show an efficient algorithm for computing this curve. Finally, we also note differences in the two types of curves are significant for algorithm design. For example, in PR space it is incorrect to linearly interpolate between points. Furthermore, algorithms that optimize the area under the ROC curve are not guaranteed to optimize the area under the PR curve.

techniques.name: Confidence Thresholding
techniques.description: Confidence thresholding uses a model score to decide whether a prediction should proceed automatically or receive different handling. For classification, a defined reject variant accepts the most likely class only when its estimated probability exceeds a chosen threshold and otherwise withholds the automatic decision. Thresholds can route withheld cases to specified review or fallback procedures, but those procedures require their own validation. Recording the score, threshold and resulting route makes the decision rule inspectable. The operating point trades automatic coverage against accepted errors, and an estimated score is not a guarantee that a decision is correct or safe.

example_use_cases.description: Implementing tiered confidence thresholds in autonomous vehicle decision-making where high-confidence lane changes (>98%) execute automatically, medium-confidence decisions (85-98%) trigger additional sensor verification, and low-confidence situations (<85%) engage conservative defensive driving modes or request human takeover.

A diabetic eye-screening service has its image classifier pass the cases it is least sure about to an ophthalmologist. The service picks the referral share, for example the least certain 10 to 20 per cent of images, so that accuracy on the cases handled automatically meets its target.

A payment processor's fraud model approves transactions it scores as clearly legitimate, runs extra automated checks on middling scores, and sends the least certain ones to an analyst. The thresholds are set so that the analyst queue stays within the team's daily capacity.

A council's tool that flags possible errors in benefit claims shows caseworkers whether each flag is above or below its confidence threshold. The council publishes the share of claims sent to manual review and the error rate among those handled automatically, so the public can see when the tool declines to decide.

limitations.description: Many models produce poorly calibrated confidence scores that don't accurately reflect true prediction uncertainty, leading to overconfident predictions for incorrect outputs or underconfident scores for correct predictions.

Threshold selection requires careful calibration and domain expertise, as inappropriate thresholds can either overwhelm human reviewers with too many cases or miss genuinely uncertain decisions that need oversight.

High-confidence predictions may still be incorrect or harmful, particularly when models encounter adversarial inputs, out-of-distribution data, or systematic biases that the confidence mechanism doesn't detect.
Static thresholds may become inappropriate over time as model performance degrades, data distribution shifts occur, or operational contexts change, requiring ongoing monitoring and adjustment.
Withholding a prediction does not make the subsequent process safe. Review delays, failed routing and inadequate fallback capacity can undermine the intended safeguard.

resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) has revolutionized the field of computer vision and image processing. In medical imaging, algorithmic solutions based on DL have been shown to achieve high performance on tasks that previously required medical experts. However, DL-based solutions for disease detection have been proposed without methods to quantify and control their uncertainty in a decision. In contrast, a physician knows whether she is uncertain about a case and will consult more experienced colleagues if needed. Here we evaluate drop-out based Bayesian uncertainty measures for DL in diagnosing diabetic retinopathy (DR) from fundus images and show that it captures uncertainty better than straightforward alternatives. Furthermore, we show that uncertainty informed decision referral can improve diagnostic performance. Experiments across different networks, tasks and datasets show robust generalization. Depending on network capacity and task/dataset difficulty, we surpass 85% sensitivity and 80% specificity as recommended by the NHS when referring 0−20% of the most uncertain decisions for further inspection. We analyse causes of uncertainty by relating intuitions from 2D visualizations to the high-dimensional image space. sample_claims.text: The vehicle's planner switches to its conservative fallback whenever perception confidence falls below the validated threshold.
Screening results the model is least certain about are referred to a clinician, and the error rate among results released without review stays within the clinical target at the chosen threshold.

techniques.name: Reject Option Classification
techniques.description: Reject Option Classification is a post-processing method, proposed by Kamiran and colleagues (2012), that changes some of a trained classifier's decisions to reduce unfair outcomes between groups, without retraining it. It defines a 'critical region' around the decision boundary, where the predicted probability is close to 50 per cent and the model is least sure. Inside that region it gives the favourable outcome to people from the disadvantaged group and the unfavourable outcome to people from the advantaged group, whatever the model predicted, and decisions outside it are left alone. The width of the region is searched on a labelled validation set, so that a chosen fairness measure, such as statistical parity difference or equal opportunity difference, falls within a set bound while accuracy stays as high as possible. The method needs each person's group at prediction time.

example_use_cases.description: A graduate recruiter's data team has a CV-scoring model whose scores near the shortlisting cut-off are the least certain. Using a labelled validation set, it searches for the narrowest band around that cut-off that brings the difference in shortlisting rates between men and women within five percentage points, and reports how many candidates' outcomes the band changes.

A hospital data science team tests the method on an unplanned-readmission alert model to narrow the gap in missed-readmission rates between insurance groups. It adopts the change only if the gap falls below five percentage points while accuracy drops by under 10 per cent and alert volume changes by under 20 per cent, and drops the method if any limit is missed.

A court service reviewing a pre-trial risk score applies the method with race as the group attribute, so that defendants whose scores sit close to the high-risk cut-off are not decided by small score differences that may reflect the model's bias. The service reports to its oversight body how many decisions the band changes, in which direction, and what it costs in accuracy.

limitations.description: Needs a model that outputs scores, because the critical region is defined on them, so a model that outputs only yes/no labels cannot be used. The scores need not be calibrated probabilities, but if they are poorly calibrated or bunched together, the wrong people fall inside the region.

Inside the region the outcome is set by group membership, so the method needs each person's group at decision time and treats people differently by group. This may be unlawful or unacceptable in some settings, such as hiring or lending, and the group attribute must be available when decisions are made.

A person from the advantaged group with a borderline score receives the unfavourable outcome, and one from the other group the favourable outcome, whatever their individual merit. A wider band closes more of the fairness gap but sets more decisions by group instead of by score, so accuracy falls as the band widens.

Cannot address bias in confident predictions outside the region. The method assumes discrimination is concentrated near the decision boundary, so where a model is confidently wrong about one group, the adjustment leaves those decisions as they are.

The band is chosen by grid search on a labelled validation set against a fairness bound (the AIF360 default is plus or minus 0.05). A small or unrepresentative validation set gives an unreliable band, and if no setting meets the bound the search returns a fallback that may not be acceptable.

resources.title: Decision Theory for Discrimination-Aware Classification
resources.abstract: Social discrimination (e.g., against females) arising from data mining techniques is a growing concern worldwide. In recent years, several methods have been proposed for making classifiers learned over discriminatory data discrimination-aware. However, these methods suffer from two major shortcomings: (1) They require either modifying the discriminatory data or tweaking a specific classification algorithm and (2) They are not flexible w.r.t. discrimination control and multiple sensitive attribute handling. In this paper, we present two solutions for discrimination-aware classification that neither require data modification nor classifier tweaking. Our first and second solutions exploit, respectively, the reject option of probabilistic classifier(s) and the disagreement region of general classifier ensembles to reduce discrimination. We relate both solutions with decision theory for better understanding of the process. Our experiments using real-world datasets demonstrate that our solutions outperform existing state-of-the-art methods, especially at low discrimination which is a significant advantage. The superior performance coupled with flexible control over discrimination and easy applicability to multiple sensitive attributes makes our solutions an important step forward in practical discrimination-aware classification.

resources.title: Exploiting reject option in classification for social discrimination control
resources.abstract: Social discrimination is said to occur when an unfavorable decision for an individual is influenced by her membership to certain protected groups such as females and minority ethnic groups. Such discriminatory decisions often exist in historical data. Despite recent works in discrimination-aware data mining, there remains the need for robust, yet easily usable, methods for discrimination control. In this paper, we utilize reject option in classification, a general decision theoretic framework for handling instances whose labels are uncertain, for modeling and controlling discriminatory decisions. Specifically, this framework permits a formal treatment of the intuition that instances close to the decision boundary are more likely to be discriminated in a dataset. Based on this framework, we present three different solutions for discrimination-aware classification. The first solution invokes probabilistic rejection in single or multiple probabilistic classifiers while the second solution relies upon ensemble rejection in classifier ensembles. The third solution integrates one of the first two solutions with situation testing which is a procedure commonly used in the court of law. All solutions are easy to use and provide strong justifications for the decisions. We evaluate our solutions extensively on four real-world datasets and compare their performances with previously proposed discrimination-aware classifiers. The results demonstrate the superiority of our solutions in terms of both performance and flexibility of applicability. In particular, our solutions are effective at removing illegal discrimination from the predictions. (C) 2017 Published by Elsevier Inc.

A fairness-focused approach to recidivism prediction: implications for accuracy, trust, and equity
resources.abstract: Fairness in AI has emerged as a critical priority, particularly in high-stakes domains like criminal justice, where algorithmic decisions profoundly affect individuals and demographic groups. This study addresses persistent challenges of bias in recidivism prediction by evaluating the integrated application of fairness-enhancing techniques across the AI pipeline. Specifically, we analyze the integrated use of Reweighing, Adversarial Learning, Disparate Impact Remover, Exponentiated Gradient Reduction, Reject Option Classification, and Equalized Odds optimization. These methods are assessed using key fairness metrics, Statistical Parity Difference (SPD), Disparate Impact (DI), Equal Opportunity Difference (EOD), and Predictive Equality Difference (PED), on two real-world recidivism datasets: COMPAS, a well-known publicly available dataset, and RisCanvi, a curated English dataset derived from a publicly available Spanish dataset. Our findings reveal trade-offs between fairness improvements and predictive accuracy, with fairness performance varying across integrated mitigation strategies. While individual techniques often fall short of effectively reducing bias, their integration across pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing stages demonstrates a more comprehensive and robust capacity to address fairness concerns. In some instances, fairness mitigation strategies exacerbate disparities instead of reducing them, highlighting the complexity of achieving equitable AI outcomes. Some methods struggle with specific datasets, leading to worsened SPD, DI, EOD, or PED values, potentially reinforcing biases rather than eliminating them. Using multi-objective and bi-objective optimization frameworks, we identify optimal configurations that balance fairness and accuracy, contributing to a deeper understanding of fairness–accuracy trade-offs in AI systems. This study makes a novel contribution by systematically evaluating multi-phase fairness integration in recidivism prediction, bridging critical gaps in the literature. However, our results also underscore the risks of ineffective or counterproductive fairness interventions when not carefully tailored. Our findings highlight the necessity of tailoring bias mitigation strategies to specific datasets and contexts, providing actionable insights for developing equitable, diverse, and inclusive AI systems that are fair and reliable in the criminal justice system.

resources.title: Evaluating Fairness Strategies in Educational Data Mining: A Comparative Study of Bias Mitigation Techniques
resources.abstract: Ensuring fairness in machine learning models applied to educational data is crucial for mitigating biases that can reinforce systemic inequities. This paper compares various fairness-enhancing algorithms across preprocessing, in-processing, and post-processing stages. Preprocessing methods such as Reweighting, Learning Fair Representations, and Disparate Impact Remover aim to adjust training data to reduce bias before model learning. In-processing techniques, including Adversarial Debiasing and Prejudice Remover, intervene during model training to directly minimize discrimination. Post-processing approaches, such as Equalized Odds Post-Processing, Calibrated Equalized Odds Post-Processing, and Reject Option Classification, adjust model predictions to improve fairness without altering the underlying model. We evaluate these methods on educational datasets, examining their effectiveness in reducing disparate impact while maintaining predictive performance. Our findings highlight tradeoffs between fairness and accuracy, as well as the suitability of different techniques for various educational applications.

sample_claims.text: On a held-out validation sample, the gap in approval rates between men and women is within the agreed bound after the critical-region adjustment, and the share of decisions the adjustment changed is reported.
Every shortlisting decision outside the critical region is the unmodified model decision. Only borderline candidates have outcomes set by group, and the share of candidates affected is reported.

After adjustment, the readmission alert model's missed-readmission rates differ by less than five percentage points between insurance groups, with accuracy and alert volume inside the limits agreed with clinicians.
The pre-trial risk tool's equal opportunity difference between racial groups is inside the stated bound on held-out cases, with the number of changed decisions reported to the oversight body.

techniques.name: Calibration with Equality of Opportunity
techniques.description: Calibration with equality of opportunity is a post-processing step that adjusts a classifier's scores so that two groups face the same error rate, in a score-based form of the equal opportunity criterion, while the scores stay calibrated. Calibrated means that, within each group, about 70% of the people given a score of 0.7 really have the outcome. The error rate is computed from the scores rather than from yes-or-no decisions, and for equality of opportunity it is how far, on average, the scores of people who truly have the outcome fall short of 1. Starting from scores already calibrated within each group, the step replaces a randomly chosen share of the scores in the group with the lower error rate by that group's overall rate of the outcome, which makes those predictions less informative until the two error rates match. Calibration is kept at a cost in accuracy for that group, and matching this score-based rate does not guarantee equal true positive rates once a decision threshold is applied.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital team finds that its follow-up screening model gives lower risk scores to women who go on to develop the condition than to men who do. Using a held-out validation set with recorded sex, it adjusts the scores so that this error is equal across the two groups, then measures the accuracy lost by the group whose scores were replaced, to decide whether the model can be released.

A university uses a model to offer extra support to students at risk of dropping out, and wants a score of 0.3 to mean about a 30% dropout rate in every fee-status group. After equalising the error rate across groups, planners plot calibration by group on held-out data to confirm the scores still mean what they say before using them to allocate support places.

limitations.description: The target can be infeasible. If even replacing every score in the lower-error group with that group's base rate leaves its error below the other group's, the two rates cannot be matched while staying calibrated. This happens when the other group's classifier is close to uninformative.

Equality is reached by making predictions worse for the group with the lower error rate, not by improving them for the other group. A random share of that group's scores is replaced by its base rate, and the loss grows with the gap between the groups' base rates.

Calibration can coexist with only one error constraint. Matching the score-based false negative rate leaves false positive rates free to diverge, so one group can face more false alarms, and equalising both while staying calibrated is impossible except in trivial cases.

Because the replaced predictions are chosen at random, two similar people in the same group can receive different outcomes. Those affected may reasonably object that a consequential decision was made by withholding information, which makes the method hard to justify in high-stakes settings.

It needs each person's group attribute when scores are adjusted, labelled held-out data to estimate how many scores to replace, and starting scores already calibrated within each group, which it preserves but cannot create. Where the attribute cannot lawfully be used, or the base model is miscalibrated, the method does not apply.

resources.title: On Fairness and Calibration
resources.abstract: The machine learning community has become increasingly concerned with the potential for bias and discrimination in predictive models. This has motivated a growing line of work on what it means for a classification procedure to be "fair." In this paper, we investigate the tension between minimizing error disparity across different population groups while maintaining calibrated probability estimates. We show that calibration is compatible only with a single error constraint (i.e. equal false-negatives rates across groups), and show that any algorithm that satisfies this relaxation is no better than randomizing a percentage of predictions for an existing classifier. These unsettling findings, which extend and generalize existing results, are empirically confirmed on several datasets.

resources.title: Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning
resources.abstract: We propose a criterion for discrimination against a specified sensitive attribute in supervised learning, where the goal is to predict some target based on available features. Assuming data about the predictor, target, and membership in the protected group are available, we show how to optimally adjust any learned predictor so as to remove discrimination according to our definition. Our framework also improves incentives by shifting the cost of poor classification from disadvantaged groups to the decision maker, who can respond by improving the classification accuracy.   In line with other studies, our notion is oblivious: it depends only on the joint statistics of the predictor, the target and the protected attribute, but not on interpretation of individualfeatures. We study the inherent limits of defining and identifying biases based on such oblivious measures, outlining what can and cannot be inferred from different oblivious tests.   We illustrate our notion using a case study of FICO credit scores.

resources.title: AIF360 demo: Calibrated Equalized Odds Postprocessing (notebook)
Evaluating Fairness Strategies in Educational Data Mining: A Comparative Study of Bias Mitigation Techniques
resources.abstract: Ensuring fairness in machine learning models applied to educational data is crucial for mitigating biases that can reinforce systemic inequities. This paper compares various fairness-enhancing algorithms across preprocessing, in-processing, and post-processing stages. Preprocessing methods such as Reweighting, Learning Fair Representations, and Disparate Impact Remover aim to adjust training data to reduce bias before model learning. In-processing techniques, including Adversarial Debiasing and Prejudice Remover, intervene during model training to directly minimize discrimination. Post-processing approaches, such as Equalized Odds Post-Processing, Calibrated Equalized Odds Post-Processing, and Reject Option Classification, adjust model predictions to improve fairness without altering the underlying model. We evaluate these methods on educational datasets, examining their effectiveness in reducing disparate impact while maintaining predictive performance. Our findings highlight tradeoffs between fairness and accuracy, as well as the suitability of different techniques for various educational applications.

techniques.name: Canary Exposure Testing
techniques.description: Canary exposure testing measures how strongly a training procedure makes a generative sequence model, such as a language model, memorise rare sequences, by planting random secrets (canaries) in the training data and scoring how much the trained model favours them over values it never saw. Because the secrets are random and their values known, the result is calibrated in a way that tests on real records are not and can be compared across model versions, training settings and numbers of repetitions; unlike extraction or membership inference testing of a finished model, it requires control of the training run, and unlike differential privacy auditing, which also plants records, it gives a memorisation score rather than a statistical bound on epsilon. The tester chooses a format such as 'my account number is' followed by a blank, fills the blank with random values to make several canaries, inserts each into the training data a chosen number of times (for example once, ten times and a hundred times), and trains with the settings used in production. Each canary is then ranked by how probable the trained model finds it compared with every other possible filling of the blank, and its exposure is the base-2 logarithm of the number of possible fillings minus the base-2 logarithm of that rank: about 1 for a canary the model treats like any other value, rising to its maximum when the canary is the model's top choice, the level at which a search over the possible fillings can extract it outright. For large spaces of values the rank is estimated by fitting a distribution to the probabilities of a sample of alternatives, and results are usually plotted as exposure against number of insertions.

example_use_cases.description: An email provider training a reply-suggestion model on users' messages inserts seven-word canaries with random middle words between 1 and 10,000 times each into a training run with the production settings, plots exposure against the number of insertions, and uses the curve to limit how often any rare phrase from a single user may appear in the training data before the model is offered to all users.

A bank's machine learning team choosing among learning-rate schedules and model sizes for an autocomplete model trained on transaction descriptions trains each candidate with the same random account-number canaries at the same insertion counts, and picks the configuration with the lowest exposure among those within a set margin of the best validation accuracy.

A health-records software vendor uses the test as a regression check: each time its clinical-text model is retrained on new notes, the same canaries are inserted at fixed frequencies, and the build fails if the exposure of a canary inserted only once rises above a threshold agreed with the vendor's information governance team.

limitations.description: It needs control of the training run. Canaries must be in the data before training, so the test cannot be applied to a model someone else trained or has already released, and it must use the production settings (optimiser, epochs, model size, hyperparameters), because each of these changes how much is memorised; a test model trained differently says little about the deployed one.

It measures memorisation of the planted secrets, not of the real data. Canaries are random and unlike the rest of the data by design, while real personal data that is repeated, structured or similar to other text can be memorised differently, and the choice of format and of random values changes the result. Low exposure for the canaries does not show that no real record can be extracted.

Exposure is not a privacy guarantee. Its scale depends on the number of possible fillings, so values compare only across canaries with the same number of fillings, and it is not an epsilon: in the original study, models trained with differential privacy at budgets too weak to mean anything (epsilon up to 10^9) still showed negligible exposure, so low exposure cannot stand in for a formal bound.

It needs the model's probability for arbitrary sequences, so a system that returns only its single best output needs a different measure. When the space of possible fillings is too large to score in full, exposure is estimated by fitting a distribution to a sample of alternatives; the estimate depends on that fit holding in the far tail and can exceed the true maximum.

techniques.name: Reliability Diagram with Expected Calibration Error
techniques.description: A reliability diagram with expected calibration error (ECE) measures whether a classifier's stated confidence matches how often it is right, so that a reader can tell whether predictions given a probability of 70 per cent come true about 70 per cent of the time. Using labelled cases the model was not trained on, each prediction's confidence (the probability given to the predicted class, or to an event such as rain above a threshold) is placed in one of a fixed number of bins, commonly ten or fifteen equal-width intervals between 0 and 1, and in each bin the average confidence is compared with the observed frequency, the share of its cases in which the predicted class or event actually occurred. The reliability diagram plots observed frequency against average confidence bin by bin, so that bins below the diagonal show overconfidence and bins above it underconfidence, and is usually shown with a histogram of how many cases fall in each bin, which the diagram itself does not show; the ECE condenses the same comparison into one number, the average gap between confidence and observed frequency weighted by each bin's share of the cases, and the maximum calibration error reports the largest gap in any bin. The technique measures and changes nothing: Platt scaling, isotonic regression calibration and temperature scaling repair a model's probabilities, and this measurement, run before and after on the same held-out cases, none of them used to fit the repair, is the evidence that a repair worked.

example_use_cases.description: A national meteorological service is deciding whether to issue a neural-network nowcast's probabilities that radar reflectivity will exceed set thresholds within the next hour. On a held-out season of radar composites, its verification team draws reliability diagrams with sample-count histograms and computes the ECE for each threshold and lead time beside those of its current extrapolation ensemble, and issues the new probabilities only for thresholds where they are at least as reliable.

A hospital's imaging AI group receives a chest X-ray classifier whose vendor reports good calibration on public data. Before connecting it, the group computes the reliability diagram and ECE on a year of its own labelled studies, finds the model overconfident in its highest bins, fits temperature scaling on a separate validation split, and repeats the measurement on the untouched test split to show whether the gap has closed.

A law firm's knowledge team evaluating a language-model research assistant that reports a confidence with each answer asks it a held-out set of questions with verified answers, bins its self-reported confidence, and computes the reliability diagram and ECE for each practice area rather than only for the whole set. The confidence display is switched off for practice areas where the gap between stated confidence and accuracy exceeds the firm's threshold.

A card issuer's fraud team checks its transaction-risk model each month on transactions whose outcomes have arrived, using bins fixed at validation that are narrow over the high scores where alerts are raised. Because fraud is rare, nearly all cases fall in the lowest bin and dominate the ECE, so the team tracks the gap in each high-score bin as well; a gap above the limit set at model sign-off triggers an investigation of drift and a decision on recalibration.

limitations.description: The result depends on how predictions are binned. With equal-width bins, confident models put most cases in one or two bins, which dominate the ECE while the others rest on few cases; more bins give a finer measurement but a noisier estimate in each bin. Rankings of recalibration methods can change with the number of bins or the binning scheme, so both must be reported and held fixed in any comparison.

Binning distorts the estimate in both directions. Overconfident and underconfident predictions in the same bin cancel, so with plenty of data the binned ECE understates the true error. On small samples, sampling noise inflates it: with 15 equal-width bins, a simulated perfectly calibrated model showed large errors on 200 cases. ECEs from samples of different sizes, such as subgroups, are not directly comparable; equal-mass bins or a debiased estimator reduce the bias.

Calibration says nothing about how well the model separates cases. A model that gives every case the overall base rate, such as 0.5 on a balanced dataset, is calibrated but useless, so the ECE must be reported with accuracy, the area under the ROC curve or a proper scoring rule such as the Brier score, which combines calibration with how decisive the predictions are.

Weighting by bin size gives rare but important predictions almost no weight. In a precipitation nowcasting study, almost all probabilities for heavy-rain thresholds fell in the lowest bin, so the ECE barely registered the rare high-probability forecasts, and at the highest threshold it could not be compared because some bins were empty. For multi-class models the usual ECE also looks only at the top predicted class and ignores the calibration of the others.

The measurement holds only for the population and period it was computed on. One ECE over a whole test set can hide large differences between subgroups: in an evaluation of language models answering medical questions, ECE ranged from 0.041 to 0.141 across specialties, a spread the pooled figure masked. Calibration can also drift after deployment, so it has to be measured for the subgroups that matter and repeated on new labelled data.

On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Confidence calibration -- the problem of predicting probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood -- is important for classification models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. Through extensive experiments, we observe that depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normalization are important factors influencing calibration. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art architectures with image and document classification datasets. Our analysis and experiments not only offer insights into neural network learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling -- a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling -- is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions.

Calibration of Self-Reported Confidence and Accuracy of Large Language Models in Medical Question Answering
resources.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the alignment between self-reported confidence of large language models (LLM) and their accuracy in answering medical multiple-choice questions. Materials and Methods: We prompted six LLMs (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 2.5) to answer MedMCQA items and report confidence scores. Based on 12,000 LLM responses, we calculated Expected Calibration Errors (ECE) by averaging absolute differences between observed accuracy and predicted confidence. Results: Mean ECE differed by model (Claude Sonnet 4.5 best: 0.06; Gpt-4o worst: 0.127) and varied across specialties (“Skin” best: 0.041; “Social & Preventive Medicine” worst: 0.141). Accuracy of examined LLMs showed analogous variation between specialties. Discussion: Our results demonstrate that high accuracy does not guarantee reliable uncertainty estimation. We identified substantial heterogeneity across medical specialties, where pooled metrics masked a threefold ECE increase between best- and worst-performing domains. Conclusion: We recommend incorporating calibration reporting into LLM evaluations, as larger models exhibit improved “self-knowledge”, but uneven overconfidence persists.

sample_claims.text: On the held-out 2025 convective season, the nowcast's probabilities of exceeding 25 dBZ at 30-minute lead time have an expected calibration error below 0.01 over ten equal-width bins, no higher than that of the current extrapolation ensemble.

After temperature scaling, the chest X-ray classifier's expected calibration error on the hospital's untouched test split is below 0.03 with 15 equal-width bins, and no bin holding more than 2 per cent of studies shows a gap above five percentage points.
For each practice area with at least 300 evaluation questions, the research assistant's self-reported confidence has an expected calibration error below 0.08 against verified answers.

In every month of 2026, in each high-score bin fixed at model sign-off, the fraud model's average predicted probability was within two percentage points of the observed fraud rate among transactions with confirmed outcomes.

techniques.name: Continuous Ranked Probability Score
techniques.description: The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) measures the quality of a probabilistic forecast of a numerical quantity, such as tomorrow's temperature or next week's demand, by scoring the whole predicted distribution, not just a single best guess, against the value later observed. For each case it compares the forecast's cumulative distribution (the predicted probability that the outcome will fall below each possible value) with a step that jumps from 0 to 1 at the observed value, squares the gap at every value and adds these up, which is the same as adding up the Brier score of the yes-or-no forecasts 'the outcome will be below this value' over every possible threshold. For a forecast given as an ensemble or a sample it can be computed as the average distance between the members and the observation minus half the average distance between pairs of members, closed forms exist for common distributions such as the Gaussian, and for a single-value forecast it reduces to the absolute error, so probabilistic and deterministic forecasts can be compared directly. The score is proper: a forecaster expects the best score by reporting the distribution they actually believe, so it cannot be improved on average by making forecasts narrower or wider than warranted, and it is lowest when the forecast distribution matches how outcomes actually vary. Scores are averaged over many cases, are in the units of the forecast quantity with lower values better, and are often reported as a skill score relative to a reference forecast such as climatology (the long-run historical distribution), giving evidence for claims about the accuracy of a forecaster's probabilities by variable, location and lead time.

example_use_cases.description: A national weather service deciding whether to run a machine-learning ensemble alongside its physics-based ensemble scores both against a year of station observations, computing the fair CRPS (the two ensembles differ in size) for 2-metre temperature and 10-metre wind at every station and lead time. It adopts the new system only for the variables and lead times where its CRPS skill relative to the existing ensemble is positive.

A wind-farm operator choosing between two vendors of probabilistic power forecasts for day-ahead trading receives 19 quantiles per hour from each. It approximates each forecast's CRPS by averaging the quantile scores across those levels and compares the vendors over a full winter against metered output. Because high-output hours drive balancing costs, it also compares them on a version of the score weighted towards the upper quantiles, averaged over all hours, not only those with high output.

A hospital group's capacity team plans elective admissions with a probabilistic forecast of bed occupancy one week ahead. Each week it computes the forecast's CRPS against the occupancy that followed and its skill score against a seasonal naive forecast, and a rolling eight-week skill score below zero triggers a review of the model before it is used for the next planning cycle.

limitations.description: One CRPS value combines calibration (whether outcomes behave like draws from the forecast distribution) and sharpness (how narrow the forecast is), so a better score does not show which improved, and an average over many cases can hide conditions in which forecasts are consistently too narrow or too wide. A claim about calibration needs Hersbach's decomposition of the score into reliability and resolution parts, a rank histogram or a spread-skill check as well.

Every threshold carries equal weight and extreme outcomes are rare, so the average score says little about how well extremes are forecast; WeatherBench 2 notes that the CRPS does not specifically focus on extreme weather. Averaging only over cases in which an extreme occurred does not repair this and can discredit skilful forecasters (Lerch et al. 2017); claims about warnings of extremes need a threshold-weighted CRPS that emphasises the tails.

It scores one quantity at one place and lead time at a time, so it does not test whether a forecast gets the relationships between places, times or variables right. WeatherBench 2 notes that its CRPS results ignore spatial and temporal correlation, and found models trained on each wind component separately biased in wind speed; claims about joint quantities, such as rainfall totalled over a catchment, need a multivariate score such as the energy score.

The score is in the units of the forecast quantity and grows with how variable that quantity is, so raw values cannot be compared or pooled across variables, locations or seasons with different variability, and averages are dominated by the most variable cases. Comparisons across these need a skill score relative to a stated reference forecast, and the choice of reference, such as climatology or persistence, changes the result.

For an ensemble, the usual estimate treats the members as the whole forecast distribution, which penalises small ensembles: if two systems draw members from the same distribution, the one with fewer members scores worse on average. Ferro (2014) showed the usual ensemble CRPS is unfair in this sense and gave an adjusted fair version, which libraries such as scoringrules provide; it should be used whenever ensembles of different sizes are compared.
